title: e2e-embed-latency-scratch-isla
body:
Purpose:
Quick personal scratchpad to capture an end-to-end embedding latency investigation for medium-size payloads (doc arrays ~750 tokens). Goal is to isolate where time is being spent: client->edge, network, pre/post-processing, model forward, postprocessing + indexing write. Want actionable knobs for reducing 95/99 p-latency for embeddings API.

Environment / config:
- date: 2025-02-19 to 2025-02-20 (runs span both days)
- cluster: hosted-prod, region: us-west-2, instance pool: embed-x1 (A10-like)
- model: open-embedding-small-v2 (fp16, ggml-quantized in dedicated tests)
- client: nodejs-sdk v0.9.3, http keepalive enabled, gzip request body
- batch handling: client-side pack up to N items (variable per test), server does dynamic micro-batching (max batch 32)
- payload: single-document embedding requests and small multi-doc arrays (1, 4, 8 docs)
- concurrency sweep: 1, 4, 8, 16 client workers (each issues requests at constant rate)
- measurement: synthetic timestamps (client send, server recv, model start, model end, server send, client recv). p50/p95/p99 computed per-run.

Quick methodology notes (informal):
- Use both real client traces and synthetic replay to separate client scheduling noise.
- Pin one run where client and server are colocated (same AZ) to measure minimal network noise.
- Collect and sample a few raw traces to inspect pre/post tokenization cost (we observed tokenization sometimes > 5ms for long docs).

Run summary (high-level):
1) Single-doc, single-concurrency (baseline): p50=12ms, p95=28ms, p99=54ms.
   - Breakdown (median of medians): client->server 2ms, preproc/tokenize 4ms, model forward 3ms, postproc+serialize 2ms, network+io jitter 1ms.
2) 4-doc batched single-concurrency (client packs 4 small docs into one request): p50=22ms, p95=45ms, p99=88ms.
   - Observed per-doc amortized forward less than single but serialization and vector concat overhead adds ~6-12ms.
3) Single-doc x8 concurrency (8 workers, no client batching): p50=40ms, p95=120ms, p99=310ms (severe tail).
   - Traces show queuing delays on server scheduling and occasional context-switch stalls in model executor (spikes align with GPU kernel queues).
4) 4-doc batched x8 concurrency: p50=60ms, p95=180ms, p99=410ms.
   - Tail worse than expected; batching increased throughput but introduced a longer tail due to partial-batch flushes and preproc variance.
5) Co-located AZ test (same AZ, reduced network variance): p50s shave ~1-2ms off, p95 ~5-10ms improvement, p99 up to ~30ms improvement in high-concurrency cases.

Interesting trace examples / anomalies:
- Several p99 traces show server-side "serialize->index-write" blocking for 60+ms when the downstream index shard was under GC/flush. Index write latency correlates with p99 spikes.
- Tokenization for long-ish docs (700-900 tokens) is variable and seems to link to Python tokenization code path hitting a slow path (fallback to regex-based). Need profiling.
- There are occasional micro-pauses (~8-15ms) recorded between model forward and postproc that correlate with CPU-to-GPU transfer reuse logic (copy fallback path).

Quick micro-experiments I ran:
A) Disabled client-side batching (always send single doc). Result: lower p99 at high concurrency (approx 20% improvement) because server-side partial-batch flushing behavior caused head-of-line blocking.
B) Increased server batch timeout from 5ms -> 10ms. Result: better throughput, p50 improved, but p99 slightly worse (more queuing visible). Tradeoff: choose p99 vs cost.
C) Switched to streaming index writes (async): p99 reduced significantly for many spikes, indexing still sometimes backpressures but less blocking on main request path.
D) Replaced tokenization path to the CPython native tokenizer for a subset of requests: tokenization variance dropped by ~60% (need to A/B larger).

Numbers (representative single-run table, rough):
- config: 8 workers, client-batch=1, server-batch-timeout=5ms
  throughput (req/s): 220
  p50: 40ms
  p95: 120ms
  p99: 310ms
  cpu% on preprocess pod: 72% (spiky)
  gpu-util: 58% (bursty), kernel-queue-latency: median 1.5ms, 95th 45ms

- config: 8 workers, client-batch=4, server-batch-timeout=10ms
  throughput (req/s): 500
  p50: 60ms
  p95: 180ms
  p99: 410ms
  cpu% preprocess: 68%
  gpu-util: 85% (more packed), kernel-queue-latency: median 2.0ms, 95th 85ms

Conclusions / hypotheses:
- For embedding workloads with variable doc sizes, client-side batching into medium-sized requests (2-4 docs) helps throughput/cost but can worsen tail if server batching/flush policies and index write block.
- Tail is dominated by two categories: downstream index write pauses and kernel-queue stalls when many partial/fill batches compete.
- Reducing tokenization variance (native tokenizer) removes a meaningful piece of p95 noise.
- Streaming/asynchronous downstream writes dramatically reduce blocking p99 spikes.

Actionable next steps (short list):
- Run a controlled A/B with async-index-write vs sync for 72h to measure p99 reduction and index backpressure behavior (ticket MLINF-842 linked).
- Instrument tokenization paths with micro-profiling (flamegraphs) for long docs; try porting hot path to the Rust tokenizer shim.
- Experiment with adaptive batch timeout: increase timeout only when queue depth > threshold to avoid constant partial flushes.
- Add a small backpressure queue between model forward and index write to absorb GC spikes (circuit-breaker).
- Collect a larger sample of kernel-queue latencies from GPU telemetry and coordinate with infra (kernel selection/launch warmup).

Open questions / TODOs to myself:
- Is the index flush event (correlating with p99) coming from the same shard consistently? If yes, can we re-route writes?
- Can we get a synthetic run with 0 index writes (simulated ack) to measure pure inference tail?
- Should we add a tiny inline cache for tiny docs to avoid repeated index writes?

Notes-to-self: keep this informal. Share with Ravi + Mae, but keep as a working doc until we have the 72h A/B results.

References / quick links: dash + PR + ticket in metadata above.

End of scratchpad.
